extracted.intended_audience: trial judges, patent litigators, and juries (drafters of jury instructions)
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions for patent trials covering damages (lost profits, reasonable royalty, apportionment), notice/marking, standards-essential patents, and willful infringement. Intended to guide court instructions and juror fact-finding on these legal standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice via marking (public notice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice to the public in general starts from the date [the Plaintiff] [and its licensees] began to mark substantially all products that use the invention with the patent number in a consistent and continuous manner. If [the Plaintiff] [and its licensees] did not mark substantially all of those products with the patent number, then [the Plaintiff] did not provide notice in this way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notice via marking is effective even if the defendant did not see or was not aware of the notice to the public. (Cites: 35 U.S.C. § 287 and cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct notice to defendant
rubrics_metrics.description: A second way [the Plaintiff] can give notice of its patent[s] is to directly notify [the Defendant] with a specific claim that the [allegedly infringing product] infringed the [abbreviated patent number] patent. This type of notice starts from the date [the Defendant] received the notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct notice establishes the start date for liability from the date received.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of failure to provide marking or direct notice on damages timing
rubrics_metrics.description: If [the Plaintiff], before filing this lawsuit, did not provide an effective public notice by properly marking its products, and did not properly provide direct notice to [the Defendant] with a specific charge that the [allegedly infringing product] infringed, then [the Plaintiff] can only recover damages for infringement that occurred after it sued [the Defendant] on [lawsuit filing date].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limits damages recovery to post-filing if no proper marking or direct notice occurred. (Cites: 35 U.S.C. §§ 286, 287(a) and cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice note — no sales/method claims (six-year damages window)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Plaintiff and any licensees to the patent(s) never made, offered for sale, or sold any patented products (either because the Plaintiff or licensees did not sell any patented product or because only method claims are asserted), then the Plaintiff can recover damages for infringement that occurred up to six years before filing suit, even without giving notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception to marking/direct notice requirement when no products were sold or when only method claims exist; statutory six-year limit applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of damages available
rubrics_metrics.description: There are several kinds of damages that are available for patent infringement, including lost profits and reasonable royalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lost profits represent additional profits the patentee would have made 'but for' the infringement; a reasonable royalty is the amount a willing licensee would have paid just before infringement began and is the minimum recoverable amount.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits—'But for' test
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Plaintiff] must show that it is more likely than not that, but for [the Defendant]’s infringement, [the Plaintiff] would have made additional profits through the sale of all or a portion of the sales of [the allegedly infringing products] made by [the Defendant].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurors must determine what purchasers would have done in the absence of infringement; profits referred to are the plaintiff's lost profits, not the defendant's profits. (Cites case law.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit factors (framework for lost profits entitlement)
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Plaintiff] has proven its lost profits if you find that [the Plaintiff] has proven each of the following factors is more likely satisfied than not: (1) a demand for the patented product/method in the relevant market; (2) the absence of acceptable non-infringing substitutes; (3) that [the Plaintiff] had the manufacturing and marketing ability to make all or a part of the infringing sales actually made by [the Defendant]; and (4) the amount of profit that [the Plaintiff] would have made if it were not for [the Defendant]’s infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each Panduit factor must be proved by a preponderance of the evidence; case citations provided for each element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit factor—Demand for the patented product/method
rubrics_metrics.description: The first factor asks whether there was demand for the patented product/method in the relevant market. Demand can be shown by significant sales of the plaintiff's product or demand for a product that directly competes with defendant's infringing product; defendant sales may be used if the products are sufficiently similar and compete in the same market or segment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence may include plaintiff's own sales or defendant's infringing sales if similarity and market competition are shown. (Cites DePuy Spine and other cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit factor—Absence of acceptable non-infringing substitutes
rubrics_metrics.description: The second factor asks whether non-infringing, acceptable substitutes for the plaintiff's product/method competed with the defendant's infringing product/method and the impact of such substitutes on the marketplace absent defendant's sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An acceptable substitute must have one or more advantages of the patented invention important to actual buyers, must not infringe (or be licensed), and must have been available during the damages period (need not have been sold). If a substitute was not sold, the defendant must show it likely could have been designed and manufactured during the damages period. If customers would likely have purchased substitutes, plaintiff is not entitled to lost profits for those sales. (Cites cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit factor—Market share (partial lost profits when substitutes exist)
rubrics_metrics.description: If there were acceptable non-infringing substitutes, the plaintiff may still be entitled to lost profits on a portion of defendant's infringing sales by proving it competed in the same market and would have made a portion of the infringing sales at least equal to its market share but for the infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff need not prove a two-supplier market; burden is to show more likely than not that plaintiff would have made that portion of sales. (Cites cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit factor—Capacity (manufacturing and marketing ability)
rubrics_metrics.description: The third factor asks whether the plaintiff had the manufacturing and marketing ability to actually make the sales it allegedly lost due to defendant's infringement. Plaintiff must prove it could have supplied the additional products or that someone working with plaintiff could have, and that it more likely than not had the ability to market and sell those additional products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence may show plaintiff's own capacity or capacity through partners; case citations provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit factor—Amount of profit (incremental income approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff may calculate lost profits by calculating lost sales and subtracting any additional costs or expenses plaintiff would have had to pay to make the lost sales. The amount cannot be speculative but need not be proven with unerring certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lost sales minus incremental costs; citations provided on proof standard and calculation approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Price erosion damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff is entitled to recover additional damages if it can show that, but for defendant's infringement, plaintiff would have been able to charge higher prices (or would not have had to lower prices). Award may equal the difference between profits at the higher price and profits actually made at the lower price.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If price erosion damages are found, the higher price may be used in determining lost sales and profits, but any decrease in sales caused by that higher price must also be accounted for. (Cites cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost escalation damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff can recover additional damages if it can show it lost profits because its costs (e.g., additional marketing costs) increased as a result of defendant's infringement. Plaintiff must prove it is more likely than not that costs rose because of defendant's actions and not for another reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires causation linking cost increases to infringement; case law cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convoyed (collateral) sales damages
rubrics_metrics.description: If plaintiff's product is ordinarily sold along with related collateral products, plaintiff may seek damages for lost sales of collateral products. To recover, plaintiff must prove (1) it more likely than not would have sold the collateral products but for the infringement, and (2) the collateral products and the product/method are so closely related that they effectively act or are used together for a common purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damages for lost collateral sales are calculated the same way as lost profits on the main product; case citations provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty—general principle
rubrics_metrics.description: If plaintiff has not proven lost profits for some or all infringing sales, the jury must consider a reasonable royalty, typically calculated by applying a royalty rate to a royalty base. The reasonable royalty must be enough to compensate for the infringement and is the minimum amount recoverable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reasonable royalty can be lump sum or running royalty; award must be based on incremental value the patented invention adds to the end product and reflect value attributable to infringing features only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty—'hypothetical negotiation' method
rubrics_metrics.description: A reasonable royalty is the royalty that would have resulted from a hypothetical license negotiation between plaintiff and defendant just before infringement began. Assume the parties believed the patent valid and infringed and had full knowledge of the facts surrounding the infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The hypothetical negotiation assumes both parties willing to license; jurors should consider the facts and circumstances known or reasonably foreseeable at the time. (Cites cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors relevant to the hypothetical negotiation (consider only supported factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining the type and amount of a reasonable royalty, jurors may consider evidence on the listed factors, in addition to any other economic evidence presented. [LIST ONLY THOSE FACTORS RELEVANT IN THE CASE AND PROPERLY SUPPORTED BY ADMITTED EVIDENCE.]
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only consider those factors that are relevant in the particular case and supported by evidence. The instructions list multiple enumerated factors (see separate entries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Royalty factor: any royalties received by the licensor (established royalty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any royalties received by the licensor for the licensing of the patent-in-suit, proving or tending to prove an established royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of prior royalties may show an established royalty rate for the technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royalty factor: rates paid by defendant for comparable patents
rubrics_metrics.description: The rates paid by [the Defendant] to license other patents comparable to the [abbreviated patent number] patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparable license rates provide a benchmark; comparability and differences must be assessed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royalty factor: nature and scope of the license
rubrics_metrics.description: The nature and scope of the license, as exclusive or non-exclusive, or as restricted or non-restricted in terms of territory or with respect to whom the manufactured product may be sold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: License scope (exclusive/non-exclusive, territory, field-of-use restrictions) affects appropriate royalty rate/structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royalty factor: licensor's policy and marketing to preserve exclusivity
rubrics_metrics.description: The licensor's established policy and marketing program to maintain its right to exclude others from using the patented invention by not licensing others to use the invention, or by granting licenses under special conditions designed to preserve that exclusivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of a licensor's licensing strategy and desire to preserve exclusivity may affect royalty valuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royalty factor: commercial relationship between licensor and licensee
rubrics_metrics.description: The commercial relationship between the licensor and the licensee, such as whether or not they are competitors in the same territory in the same line of business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competitive relationships influence bargaining positions in the hypothetical negotiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royalty factor: effect of patented product on other sales (collateral sales)
rubrics_metrics.description: The effect of selling the patented product/method in promoting other sales of the licensee; the existing value of the invention to the licensor as a generator of sales of its non-patented items; and the extent of such collateral sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value as a driver of collateral sales should be considered when assessing royalty value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royalty factor: duration of patent and term of license
rubrics_metrics.description: The duration of the patent and the term of the license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remaining patent life and length of the hypothetical license influence royalty amounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royalty factor: established profitability, commercial success, popularity
rubrics_metrics.description: The established profitability of the product made under the patent; its commercial success; and its popularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial success and profitability are indicia of value in the hypothetical negotiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royalty factor: utility and advantages over prior modes/devices
rubrics_metrics.description: The utility and advantages of the patented invention over the old modes or devices, if any, that had been used for achieving similar results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical advantages that matter to buyers strengthen bargaining position for higher royalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royalty factor: nature and commercial embodiment of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The nature of the patented invention; the character of the commercial embodiment of it as owned and produced by or for the licensor; and the benefits to those who have used the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how the invention is embodied commercially and the benefits users obtain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royalty factor: extent of defendant's use and value of that use
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which [the Defendant] has made use of the invention; and any evidence that shows the value of that use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Degree of use by defendant is relevant to apportionment and royalty magnitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royalty factor: customary portion of profit or selling price in the business
rubrics_metrics.description: The portion of the profit or of the selling price that may be customary in the particular business or in comparable businesses to allow for the use of the invention or analogous inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industry customs on profit splits for use of technologies can inform reasonable royalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royalty factor: portion of profit attributable to the patented invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The portion of the profit that arises from the patented invention itself as opposed to profit arising from unpatented features, such as the manufacturing process, business risks, or significant features or improvements added by the accused infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apportion royalty to value of patented features only; distinguish from profits due to other factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royalty factor: opinion testimony of qualified experts
rubrics_metrics.description: The opinion testimony of qualified experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert economic and industry testimony may be considered in setting a reasonable royalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royalty factor: bargaining outcome a prudent licensee and patentee would accept
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount that a licensor and a licensee would have agreed upon at the time the infringement began if both sides were reasonably and voluntarily trying to reach an agreement; i.e., the amount a prudent licensee would pay and a willing patentee would accept to allow reasonable profit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This synthesizes economic realities and bargaining positions at the hypothetical negotiation date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royalty factor: any other economic factor a prudent businessperson would consider
rubrics_metrics.description: Any other economic factor that a normally prudent business person would, under similar circumstances, take into consideration in negotiating the hypothetical license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permits consideration of additional relevant economic evidence beyond enumerated factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution/Apportionment of royalty (value to patented features only)
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount you find as a reasonable royalty must be based on the value attributable to the patented features, as distinct from other, unpatented features of the accused product, or other factors such as marketing or advertising and the defendant's size or market position. The ultimate combination of both the royalty rate and the royalty base must reflect the value attributable to the patented technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not choose a royalty base that is too high and then downward-adjust by rate, or vice versa. Determine an appropriate base and rate that together reflect value of patented invention alone. (Cites cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Entire Market Value Rule (EMVR) and smallest salable unit
rubrics_metrics.description: Royalties for multi-component products should be based not on the entire product but on the 'smallest salable unit' that practices the patented invention and has close relation to the claimed invention. If that unit contains non-infringing features unrelated to the patented feature(s), damages must be based only on the portion of that unit's value attributable to the patented technology. The EMVR is a narrow exception allowing use of entire product revenues only if the patented feature is the sole driver of customer demand or substantially creates product value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EMVR is narrow and requires plaintiff to show patented feature drives demand for the entire product. May involve estimating feature value that was never separately sold. (Cites cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty—multiple patents
rubrics_metrics.description: If defendant infringed multiple patents, and if a reasonable royalty is awarded, separate royalties may be awarded for each patent infringed. Jurors may consider evidence of how many patent licenses are needed for the product and the effect on the hypothetical negotiation of paying royalties for each license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider cumulative licensing burden and how multiple patents affect hypothetical bargaining. (Cites cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty—timing (no hindsight but foreseeable facts allowed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages are not based on a hindsight evaluation but on what the parties to the hypothetical license negotiations would have agreed upon at the time. Evidence relevant to the negotiation is not necessarily limited to facts on or before that date; jurors may consider information the parties would have foreseen or estimated, which under certain circumstances may include post-infringement usage, licenses entered shortly after the negotiation date, infringer profits, and non-infringing alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permits some forward-looking or reasonably foreseeable evidence but anchors valuation to the hypothetical negotiation date. (Cites cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty—availability of non-infringing substitutes
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining a reasonable royalty, jurors may consider evidence concerning the availability and cost of acceptable non-infringing substitutes to the patented invention. An acceptable substitute must be licensed under the patent or not infringe the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Availability and cost of substitutes affect bargaining and royalty valuation. (Cites cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty—use of comparable license agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurors may consider amounts other parties have paid for rights to the patent(s) or comparable technologies and the structures of such payments. A license need not be perfectly comparable to be considered, but differences must be accounted for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When relying on prior licenses, adjust for differences in technology and economic circumstances between those agreements and the hypothetical license. (Cites cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Doubts about damages resolved against infringer (failure to keep records)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any doubts jurors may have on the issue of damages due to defendant's failure to keep proper records should be decided in favor of the plaintiff. Confusion or difficulties caused by defendant's records or lack of records should be held against the defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If records are missing or inadequate, jurors may resolve ambiguities against the party who failed to keep them. (Cites cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard-Essential Patents (SEPs) practice note — FRAND and apportionment
rubrics_metrics.description: Regarding SEPs, the jury must be instructed on the particulars of the FRAND commitment made by the patentee, established principles of patent law, and only those Georgia-Pacific factors relevant in the case. The jury must be instructed that any royalty for a SEP must be based on the incremental value of the claimed invention (or approximate value) and apportioned to the value of the claimed invention, not the value of the standard as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not instruct jurors on irrelevant Georgia-Pacific factors. Emphasize apportionment and that royalties should not be based on the value of the entire standard. (Cites cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful infringement—general standard
rubrics_metrics.description: If jurors find defendant infringed a valid claim, they must determine whether the infringement was willful. To show willfulness, plaintiff must prove it is more likely than not that defendant knew of plaintiff's patent and intentionally infringed at least one asserted claim. Jurors may consider whether defendant's behavior was deliberate or intentional, but knowledge alone is not sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess totality of circumstances and defendant's knowledge at the time of the challenged conduct. A finding of willfulness does not affect the amount of damages the jury awards, but willfulness may be considered later. (Cites Halo and other cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful infringement—reliance on legal opinion (35 U.S.C. § 298)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice note: the AIA eliminated failure to obtain an opinion of counsel as a factor in determining willfulness (35 U.S.C. § 298). If defendant relies on a legal opinion, jurors may consider whether defendant reasonably relied on a competent legal opinion as one factor in the totality of circumstances. If defendant does not rely on an opinion, jurors should not assume absence of counsel means the opinion would have been unfavorable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurors may consider reasonable reliance on competent counsel as one factor but cannot use absence of counsel as proof of willfulness; modify instruction depending on whether defendant asserts reliance on an opinion. (Cites § 298 and Halo.)
